frontier_question: Why did a US court find Google's search business a monopoly, and what remedies were ordered?

chunks.content: Judge Amit Mehta (US District Court for the District of Columbia) ruled on 2024-08-05 that Google is a monopolist in general search services and general search text advertising, violating Section 2 of the Sherman Act. The theory of harm was default-distribution deals: Google paying Apple, Samsung, Mozilla and others billions to be the default search engine — Google's CEO Sundar Pichai testified the company paid about $26.3 billion for distribution in 2021, and trial evidence showed Google paid Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue. On 2025-08-05, Judge Mehta ordered structural remedies: Google must sell Chrome (the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case of 2000), may no longer pay for default search placement (no revenue-sharing agreements), and faces limits on acquisitions and AI-related investments. The ruling established that paying for default placement in search distribution is exclusionary conduct — defaults create scale, scale creates data, data creates quality, quality protects the default, a self-reinforcing loop rivals could not break. Google appealed to the DC Circuit (notice filed 2025), arguing the trial court punished procompetitive innovation; the case's final outcome remained pending through 2025.

Judge Amit Mehta ruled on August 5, 2024, that these practices allowed Google to maintain its dominance in general search services and text advertising [Source: ev-1].

The core theory of harm was that Google paid billions of dollars to companies like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to be their default search engine; for instance, CEO Sundar Pichai testified that Google spent approximately $26.3 billion on distribution in 2021, and trial evidence indicated Google paid Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue [Source: ev-1].
This created a self-reinforcing loop where paying for defaults generated scale, which led to more data, improved quality, and protected the default status against rivals [Source: ev-1].

On August 5, 20 has ordered structural remedies requiring Google to divest its Chrome browser—a move described as the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case in 2000—and prohibiting it from paying for default search placement through revenue-sharing agreements [Source: ev-1].
Additionally, the court imposed limits on Google's acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1].

Although Google appealed this decision to the DC Circuit Court of Appeals in 2025, arguing that the ruling punished procompetitive innovation, the final outcome remained pending throughout 2025 [Source: ev-1].
